title: Monitoring Training and Recovery during a Period of Increased Intensity or Volume in Recreational Endurance Athletes
authors: Nuuttila OP, Nummela A, Häkkinen K, Seipäjärvi S, Kyröläinen H
journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
population: Recreationally trained participants: 10-week control period then 10 weeks of increased intensity (INT, n=13) or volume (VOL, n=17)
findings: Thirty recreationally trained participants did a 10-week control period of regular training and then a 10-week period of increased intensity (INT, n=13) or volume (VOL, n=17).
Both groups improved maximal treadmill speed (INT 3.4 +/- 3.2%, p<0.001; VOL 2.1 +/- 1.8%, p=0.006), to a similar extent.

The only between-group difference in monitoring variables was nocturnal HR (p=0.013), which decreased in INT (p=0.016); perceived recovery decreased in VOL (p=0.021) and tended to decrease in INT (p=0.056).
Countermovement jump and HRV remained unaffected despite a slight decrease in perceived recovery.

The increase in the heart rate-running speed index at the end of the period was greater in responders than low-responders (p=0.005); authors say long-term HR-RS monitoring may help predict positive adaptation, while other recovery markers need individualized interpretation.
limitations: Small sample; allocation method is not stated in the abstract; recreational athletes, 10 weeks; not a test of recovery-week frequency; few effect sizes reported.
implications: Progressive intensity or progressive volume yield similar treadmill-speed gains (about 2-3%) over 10 weeks in recreational athletes, so the generator may choose the lever that fits the athlete's time.
Track an HR-to-speed efficiency index across weeks as a positive-adaptation indicator and use perceived recovery as a cue; do not use resting HRV or jump tests as decision signals.

verification.notes: Crossref and PubMed match (IJERPH 2021;18(5):2401). Removed the researcher's 'non-randomized' (not stated in abstract) and corrected the nocturnal HR p-values.
